title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is a case of AI-generated impersonation used as a component of investment fraud. Scammers fabricated a realistic-looking interview article featuring two named public figures, a central bank governor and a finance broadcaster, neither of whom participated in any such interview. The AI tools involved appear to have been used to produce convincing text and, by implication, supporting material including fake websites, reviews, and news articles. The failure is not in a deployed AI product from a legitimate company but in the offensive use of generative AI by bad actors to manufacture credibility at scale.

The mechanism works because the output looks professionally produced. A reader encountering the article has no visible signal that it is synthetic, and the elaborate supporting infrastructure of fake reviews and websites is designed to remove further doubt. Catching it would require either prior knowledge that the interview never happened, cross-referencing the named individuals' actual public records, or checking the licensing status of the promoted platform against an official register. None of those checks happen automatically for an ordinary consumer.

What is not established is the identity of those responsible, the scale of financial harm caused to individuals, or whether any specific AI product or platform was used to generate the material. ASIC's figures describe the broader trend of removals and are a regulatory report, not a court finding.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has become the latest example of AI-generated investment scams rapidly increasing in Australia. The fictional interview promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, and depicted Bullock becoming upset during questioning about the service. The article and interview never actually occurred, but similar schemes are becoming increasingly common and sophisticated as generative artificial intelligence technology advances.

Australia's financial regulator ASIC reports a significant rise in these deceptive practices, removing 19,400 scams last year, up 182 percent from the previous year. The watchdog identified 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Politicians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and celebrities like Alan Kohler and Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated Australians in these schemes. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers and warns that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy. Scammers often create elaborate deception networks with fake websites, reviews and news articles to build credibility before requesting personal details.
